2610.40774.abstract: Uncovering the origins of merging binary black holes is a key goal in gravitational-wave astrophysics, but identifying the formation channel of a particular binary is complicated by imprecise measurements and uncertain theoretical predictions. While classification often involves computing metrics from an event's inferred properties, measurement precision varies across parameter space. Using the perhaps-surprising low masses of the hierarchical merger candidates GW241011 and GW241110 as a backdrop, we consider the classifiable distribution, which steps beyond detectability to assess what events may be correctly characterized as part of a population. Interpreting classification outcomes, and assessing the falsifiability of theoretical model predictions, are benefit by understanding the regions of parameter space that a priori enable---and do not enable---confident measurement. For hierarchical mergers, we demonstrate that mass ratio is the largest intrinsic driver of identification, while orbital inclination and signal-to-noise ratio are the key extrinsic factors. Further, we show GW241011 and GW241110 achieve classification metrics consistent with similar simulated hierarchical mergers. Model selection and classification require the context of measurement capacity, especially as catalogs offer growing numbers of events with seemingly unusual properties.

2610.40782.abstract: The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) collaboration has detected two binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, GW170817 and GW190425. While no clear electromagnetic counterpart was discovered for GW190425, a coincident counterpart to GW170817 (GRB170817A, AT 2017gfo) was discovered in an early-type galaxy, NGC 4993. Using broad-band photometry and an integrated optical spectrum, we measure a mass-weighted age of $12.4^{+0.5}_{-0.7}$ Gyr (90% credible) for NGC 4993, which is an estimate of the delay time between star formation and merger for the GW170817 progenitor. BNS systems are expected to have a power-law delay-time distribution (DTD) with a minimum delay time, $t_{\rm min}$, of ~10 Myr and index $\alpha \approx -1$. This canonical DTD, convolved with the cosmic star-formation history, predicts ~16 BNS mergers at delay times of ~100 Myr for every BNS merger at 10 Gyr; under it, the chance of detecting even one merger as old as GW170817 is ~1.8%. The long delay time of GW170817 therefore implies many "missing" shorter-delay mergers if the canonical DTD holds. A DTD with $t_{\rm min} = 12.6$ Gyr and $\alpha = -1$ is favored over the canonical DTD by a factor of 40-140, and over short gamma-ray burst and Galactic double-NS DTDs by factors of 80-280. These results are in tension with current population synthesis models, the Milky Way double NS population, and the SGRB population. Explaining the LVK population requires either a dramatically different separation distribution than commonly assumed, an additional channel with a long delay time and comparable rate to an isolated-binary formation scenario, or a large population of BNS mergers missed in the LVK analysis. This result has wide-ranging implications for binary-population synthesis, chemical enrichment models, connections between BNS mergers and SGRBs, and future gravitational wave observations.

2610.40787.abstract: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) disks are promising sites for hierarchical binary black hole (BBH) mergers, which next-generation gravitational-wave detectors will probe out to high redshift. Predicting their contribution requires linking BBH evolution in AGN disks to the poorly constrained high-redshift evolution of active supermassive black holes (SMBHs). We introduce ARISE (AGN Rates and Intrinsic Stellar-BH Evolution), a framework that embeds semi-analytical models of BBH evolution in AGN disks into a cosmological description of the AGN number density, SMBH mass function, Eddington-ratio distribution, and nuclear metallicity. We consider a conservative AGN-abundance model anchored to observed luminosity functions, as well as Eddington-limited and super-Eddington scenarios based on the CAT cosmological model, compatible with JWST observations of high-redshift AGNs. The merger-rate density is set primarily by the disk viscosity parameter $\alpha$: at $z = 0.2$, we find a rate of $12$--$37$ Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$ for $\alpha = 0.01$ and $0.5$--$6$ Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$ for $\alpha = 0.1$. The redshift evolution depends strongly on how SMBHs grow. The rate density peaks at $z \simeq 1.8$, $3.3$, and $3.9$ ($1.5$, $3.6$, and $3.9$) for $\alpha=0.01$ ($0.1$) in the conservative, Eddington-limited, and super-Eddington models, respectively, and in the super-Eddington model it stays nearly flat out to $z \simeq 10$. For $\alpha = 0.1$, AGN disks account for $\sim 2$--$40\%$ of the LVK-inferred merger rate, consistent with current upper limits from GW--AGN associations. For $\alpha = 0.01$, they match or exceed it. The Einstein Telescope (ET) should detect $\sim 10^{5}$ ($\sim 10^{4}$) AGN-disk mergers per year for $\alpha = 0.01$ ($0.1$). ET will test the AGN channel at redshifts where the AGN population models differ most strongly, providing independent constraints on the growth of early SMBHs.

2610.40907.abstract: Identifying the astrophysical sites of the heavy rapid neutron-capture process ($r$-process) remains one of the most prominent unsolved problems in nuclear astrophysics. Emitted $\gamma$-rays from the decay of unstable nuclei have been identified as a potential observable marker on both prompt and delayed timescales which could provide conclusive evidence of the presence of $r$-process activity. In this work, we identify and discuss the importance of $^{250}$Cm to the $\gamma$-ray spectra of remnants, showing that the decay spectrum of $^{250}$Cm dominates the $\gamma$-ray spectra of $r$-process ejecta across a broad timescale ($\sim$ 2,000 - 20,000 years). We highlight the uncertain nature of this spectra: $^{250}$Cm may decay via $\alpha$-decay, $\beta$-decay, and spontaneous fission, but the decay branchings are not experimentally known, and each decay channel produces unique spectral lines which may be observable. We examine the potential for observation of the most prominent spectral signatures, finding that for conventional neutron star merger remnants, $\gamma$-ray lines will be detectable in current and future detectors only in the very near galaxy ($\sim$ 1 kpc), but other sites which could produce a larger ejecta mass may have greater observable distances. Our findings highlight the potential of actinide decay chains to indicate r-process nucleosynthesis and further underscore the necessity of measuring the nuclear properties that define their characteristic spectral signatures.

2610.40958.abstract: Prompt millisecond-duration coherent radio emission is proposed as a counterpart to neutron-star-containing compact mergers, produced before, during, or shortly after coalescence. Its detection would probe the plasma environment, magnetic fields, remnant evolution, and emission physics of these mergers. At GHz frequencies, dispersive delays can range from fractions of a second to several seconds, requiring the telescope to be on source before or soon after coalescence. Negative- or low-latency alerts, rapid response, and optimized pointing under uncertain, evolving localizations are therefore essential. We present a framework for prompt gravitational-wave follow-up with the upcoming Deep Synoptic Array (DSA), a sensitive, fast-slewing, wide-field GHz radio array. We simulate low-latency localization sequences and embed them in a follow-up environment with elevation, field-of-view, and slew constraints. We compare a reinforcement-learning pointing policy with a baseline that slews toward the highest-probability accessible region at each step. This peak-tracking rule is a strong, interpretable baseline for initial deployment, while the learned policy provides a complementary strategy for a subset of broad, multimodal, or arc-shaped localizations. At a random merger time, 37% of events are observable above $20^\circ$ elevation; among these, $\sim90\%$ of BNS events are successfully reached and tracked using zero-noise localization maps, decreasing to $\sim75\%$ with Gaussian-noise maps. We validate the optimized pointing trajectories on prototype DSA antennas. DSA follow-up can reach a fluence sensitivity of $\sim20$ mJy ms over a representative 700-1025 MHz sub-band, probing millisecond bursts with luminosities of approximately $10^{38}$ to $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$, at or below the lower end of several coherent-emission predictions for neutron-star mergers.

2610.41005.abstract: In 2024, two new missions were launched to detect high-energy transients. EP and SVOM aim to observe soft transients from X-ray rich gamma-ray bursts (XRR), X-ray flashes (XRF), to fast X-ray transients (FXT). GRB 241113B, the first soft gamma-ray burst (GRB) jointly detected by EP and SVOM from soft X-rays to gamma-rays (0.5--1000~keV). GRB 241113B has an $E^{obs}_{peak} \approx 35$ keV and a redshift (z) likely between 0.5 and 3.5, with $T_{90,\gamma} \approx 42$~s (4--30~keV). This burst can be classified as either an XRR or XRF, depending on the fluence ratio used. The afterglow is achromatic and featureless with a normal decay ($\alpha \approx -1.40$). The prompt emission does not satisfy the shock-breakout relation, and thus a geometry comprised of a jet is preferred. However, the afterglow fitting favors a jet viewed on-axis dominated by synchrotron emission due to electrons in a slow cooling regime, interacting with a wind medium. The bulk Lorentz factor ($\Gamma$) indicates that the motion of the jet is ultrarelativistic ($\Gamma_{0}>100$), which discards the dirty fireball model. Hence, the jet baryon loading should be compatible with that of classical GRBs (C-GRBs). The prompt spectral properties of GRB 241113B ($\alpha$, $E^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{peak}}$, $E_{\gamma,iso}$) are comparable to those of XRFs/XRRs and are in the continuity of the C-GRB distributions, setting it apart from the extragalatic FXT population solely detected by EP. Hence, the SVOM mission, with the benefit brought by the instrument ECLAIRs with its high sensitivity and low energy threshold (at 4keV), is able to detect the potential $\gamma$-ray counterpart of soft transients also observed by EP and help to differentiate them from FXTs. The latter show the interest of the joint operation of both missions to better study the landscape of soft transients.

2610.41119.abstract: We present MAGIKS, a multimodal framework for gravitational-wave (GW)-triggered kilonova identification that formulates counterpart search as query-conditioned gallery retrieval. Following an align-before-fuse design, MAGIKS combines GW source parameters and sky-localization maps with irregularly sampled multiband optical light curves and sky coordinates. A time-aware supervised contrastive objective provides coarse cross-modal alignment, while dual cross-attention evaluates consistency between optical coordinates and GW localization, and between GW parameters and optical evolution. We train and evaluate MAGIKS on simulated binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole mergers, Rubin Observatory kilonova light curves from regular survey observations and target-of-opportunity follow-up, GW-detected mergers without Rubin-detectable kilonova counterparts, and realistic non-kilonova contaminants. In independent galleries with one true counterpart and time- and sky-compatible distractors, MAGIKS outperforms optical-only and sky-localization-only ranking, with increasing gains as galleries grow. At 5000 candidates, it ranks the counterpart first for 39.8% of queries, versus 4.8% and 0.2% for these baselines. In a GW170817 study, we generate counterfactual Rubin observations using released GW parameters and three-dimensional localization, the measured counterpart position, and host distance. At the same gallery size, MAGIKS achieves top-1 and top-10 retrieval rates of 87.3% and 95.7%. It correctly classifies 94.2% of associated and non-associated GW-optical pairs. In a separate crossed-pair experiment, its matching score responds significantly to controlled changes in all five tested GW parameters. These results support GW-conditioned kilonova candidate prioritisation for future multi-messenger follow-up.

2610.41163.abstract: Local star-forming regions have recently been the subject of scrutiny as cosmic-ray accelerators and sources of ultra-high-energy gamma-ray emissions. The Cygnus-X region is one of the richest star forming regions in the galaxy and over the last few decades has been extensively studied. Here we report the detection of a star-forming region located in the southern part of Cygnus-X, Sharpless 106 (S106), using the HAWC Observatory. The S106 region is spatially located near the cataloged gamma-ray source 1LHAASO J2027+3657. In this work, we perform a multi-wavelength analysis of S106, by combining HAWC data with re-analysis of Fermi-LAT and archival Chandra data. We construct a fully leptonic model for the multi-wavelength emission from S106 from a single population of high-energy leptons, with the gamma-rays greater than 1 TeV being produced by inverse Compton scattering of the locally-produced IR photon field from S106 itself. Our models show that hadronic mechanisms are not always required to explain the observed flux from gamma-ray star-forming regions and that understanding the specific details of local photon fields is crucial to modeling the multi-wavelength emission from star-forming regions.

2610.41242.abstract: The neutron star (NS) mass distribution serves as a crucial probe of the dense matter equation of state (EOS) and core-collapse supernova explosion mechanisms. Although observations reveal a bimodal NS mass distribution, existing theoretical simulations often struggle to naturally reproduce the high-mass peak, and the impact of the quark-hadron phase transition (PT) in high-density nuclear matter remains largely unexplored. Employing the 1D general-relativistic hydrodynamics code GR1D with hybrid EOSs incorporating a first-order PT (RDF1.1 and RDF1.2), we systematically simulate core-collapse supernovae for progenitors with zero-age main-sequence masses ranging from 13 to 120 $M_\odot$. Our results reveal a threefold impact of the PT onset density on the final supernova fate: in low-compactness progenitors, an early PT truncates accretion and produces less massive NSs; in the critical-compactness regime, it facilitates successful explosions; and in high-compactness progenitors, it accelerates black hole formation. Compared with the $\sim 1.4\,M_\odot$ peak typical of the conventional core-collapse scenario, the inclusion of the PT produces NSs with masses centered around $1.70\,M_\odot$ for RDF1.1 and within $1.55$--$1.70\,M_\odot$ for RDF1.2. Furthermore, we identify a novel formation channel whereby low-compactness progenitors with failed initial shocks can form more massive NSs via a PT-induced second shock. Due to the fixed nature of the PT boundary, the final NS masses exhibit a pronounced clustering effect. This study elucidates the critical role of the quark-hadron PT in shaping the NS mass distribution, providing important astrophysical constraints on the properties of high-density nuclear matter and the formation mechanism of massive NSs.

2610.41476.abstract: The binary neutron star merger GW170817 established a direct link between gravitational waves and short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs), whose afterglows are commonly interpreted as nonthermal emission from structured relativistic jets viewed off-axis. Some sGRBs exhibit extended or plateau X-ray emission, suggesting prolonged central-engine activity. These X-ray photons can serve as seed photons for external inverse-Compton (EIC) scattering by relativistic electrons in the jet, producing very-high-energy (VHE) gamma rays. However, how the angular structure of the jet affects the detectability of EIC emission remains insufficiently explored. Here, we investigate EIC emission from off-axis structured jets and assess its detectability with the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO). We find that EIC emission powered by extended and/or plateau X-rays produces detectable VHE signals from nearby sGRBs, particularly during the early afterglow, significantly outshining synchrotron self-Compton emission. In our adopted models, Gaussian and power-law jets produce brighter off-axis EIC emission than a top-hat jet, extending the viewing-angle range over which VHE emission may be detectable. These results demonstrate that early VHE observations with CTAO can probe both prolonged central-engine activity and the angular structure of relativistic jets in sGRBs.

2610.41509.abstract: We investigate the long-term X-ray spectral evolution of the highly luminous, radio-quiet quasar PDS 456 using AstroSat observations obtained in 2019 and 2021 together with archival XMM-Newton, NuSTAR and Suzaku observations spanning 2001-2024. The AstroSat observations provide valuable coverage following the bright flaring state observed in 2018, revealing that the source underwent a relatively quiescent phase in 2019 before re-brightening in 2021. During the AstroSat epochs, PDS 456 exhibits a harder-when-brighter spectral trend, whereas the long-term XMM-Newton, NuSTAR, and Suzaku observations confirm the overall softer-when-fainter behavior. This behavior is consistent with the presence of a very cool corona (~15 keV), possibly driven by a strong incident photon field for upscattering, as suggested by a prominent big blue bump. Broadband spectral modeling of simultaneous XMM-Newton and NuSTAR observations, complemented by the 2021 AstroSat flaring epoch and interpreted within the self-consistent physical framework reXcor, indicates that the disk-corona energy balance evolves with flux. In low-flux states, the spectrum is reflection-dominated, implying efficient illumination of the inner accretion disk by a compact corona. In contrast, high-flux states show an enhanced contribution from the warm Comptonizing region at larger coronal heights. The Fe K{\alpha} emission line displays a positive correlation with the 2-10 keV continuum flux at low to intermediate flux levels, while deviations at the highest flux states suggest a reduced relative reflection contribution as the warm corona becomes energetically dominant.

2610.41729.abstract: We present well-sampled multi-band imaging and low- to medium-resolution spectroscopic observations of the early-discovered Type~II supernova (SN)~2025dys. The photometric evolution exhibits a rise time of $\sim$\,18 days ($r$ band) and a rapid decline transitioning to the radioactive decay tail at $\sim$\,70 days. SN~2025dys is among the high-luminosity events with a peak pseudo-bolometric luminosity of $L_{\rm opt}=8.57\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. Early X-ray emission was identified, displaying a luminosity of $7.55\times10^{40}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. The observational investigation points to a dense, hydrogen-rich circumstellar medium with a mass of $M_{\rm CSM}\approx0.5$--$0.7\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$, suggesting a partially stripped, hydrogen-poor inner ejecta with a relatively low mass of $M_{\rm ej}\approx2.5\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$. The explosion possessed a kinetic energy of $E_{\rm k}\approx0.3\text{--}0.5$~foe and yielded a synthesized nickel mass of $M_{\rm Ni}\approx0.042_{-0.011}^{+0.012}\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$. These physical parameters indicate an extreme mass-loss episode before the explosion, characterized by a high mass-loss rate of $\dot{M} \gtrsim 0.01\,\mathrm{M_\odot\,yr^{-1}}$. SN~2025dys represents a stripped progenitor, intrinsically resembling a Type~IIb or even a Type~Ib SN, that exploded within a dense, hydrogen-rich circumstellar environment.

2610.41734.abstract:
Her X-1 is an eclipsing X-ray binary system consisting of an accreting neutron star and an optical component HZ Her. In addition to the 1.24-s X-ray pulsations and the 1.7-d orbital period, the system also shows a 35-day X-ray variability related to the precessional motion of a tilted and twisted accretion disk around the neutron star. The long-term persistence of the 35-day X-ray variability suggests the presence of a stable clock mechanism, most likely free precession of the magnetized neutron star.
We have studied the long-term behavior of the 35-day cycle of Her X-1 using all available CGRO/BATSE, RXTE/ASM, Swift/BAT, Fermi/GBM, MAXI data and archival turn-on moments of the 35-day cycle spanning more than 50 years. We have used a sliding-window averaged X-ray phase light curve and the classical O-C (observed minus calculated) diagram for individual 35-day turn-ons to inspect the long-term trends of the O-C diagram. The O-C diagram demonstrates two similar parabolic trends separated by an anomalous low state (ALS) of the source suggesting a secular decrease in the 35-d precession period with $\dot P_\text{35} =(-1.3\pm0.2)\times10^{-5} \,\mathrm{~s\,s}^{-1}$ and $\dot P_\text{35} =(-4.7\pm0.1)\times10^{-5} \,\mathrm{~s\,s}^{-1}$ before and after the ALS, respectively.
We conclude that the decay of the 35-day period as inferred from the O-C analysis can be interpreted in terms of the direct relationship between the change of the precessional period of the accretion disk to the long-term decrease of the period of the free precessional neutron star - due to continued accumulation of accreted matter.

2610.41739.abstract: LS~5039 is a well-studied $\gamma$-ray binary exhibiting strong orbital modulation from GeV to TeV energies. We present a phase-resolved analysis of 17.3~yr of \textit{Fermi}-LAT observations and identify an additional $\gamma$-ray excess in the $\sim30$--$500$~GeV at a significance of $\sim7.9\sigma$. The phase-resolved spectra show pronounced orbital dependence above $\sim10$~GeV, with the inferior-conjunction more complex than the superior-conjunction. To investigate the broadband spectral energy distribution, we combine the \textit{Fermi}-LAT spectra with published H.E.S.S.\ and HAWC measurements and compare purely leptonic and lepto-hadronic models using the Bayesian information criterion. In both intervals, relativistic-Maxwellian and magnetospheric components dominate below $\sim10$~GeV, while shock-accelerated electrons account for much of the GeV--TeV continuum. The purely leptonic fits leave residuals at $30$--$500$~GeV and underpredict the HAWC measurements above $\sim100$~TeV. In the local one-zone intrabinary shock apex model, synchrotron cooling and Klein-Nishina suppression make the ultra-high-energy emission difficult to reproduce, although more complex leptonic scenarios remain possible. Adding a phenomenological proton component improves the broadband description, with stronger relative support during superior-conjunction than inferior-conjunction. However, the proton parameters remain weakly constrained and the fast-escape hadronic interpretation is energetically challenging, so a hadronic origin is not uniquely established. Future high-sensitivity, phase-resolved observations at multi-TeV and ultra-high energies will be required to test this interpretation.

2610.41846.abstract: We report updated mass and radius measurements for the millisecond pulsar PSR J0437-4715 obtained with pulse profile modeling of the emission from the far-ultraviolet to the hard X-rays. Using an extended 2.56 Ms Neutron Star Interior Composition ExploreR (NICER) dataset together with XMM-Newton, Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope ARray and Hubble Space Telescope observations, we perform Bayesian inference with models describing the thermal emission from hot spots of increasing complexities, together with the rest of the warm NS surface, as well as the non-thermal emission component represented by a phase-dependent (pulsed) power-law. With this comprehensive model and broadband data set, as well as radio timing priors on the mass, distance and inclination, our headline result for PSR J0437-4715 led to a mass M = 1.377(-0.034)(+0.038) Msun and an equatorial radius Req = 11.35(-0.39)(+0.40) km, one of the narrowest measurements of Req from NICER observations of millisecond pulsars. The geometric configuration favors a non-antipodal hot spot distribution, as noted in previous analyses of this pulsar. When combined with recent measurements of M and Req of other pulsars, the tight constraints from PSR J0437-4715 further reduce the allowed range of the dense matter equation of state, excluding those that predict radii above 12.0 km (at the 68% level) for all NS masses.

2610.41948.abstract: Presolar graphite grains with supernova isotopic signatures provide direct evidence that large graphite grains formed in supernova ejecta. However, theoretical calculations of dust formation in supernovae have typically predicted graphite grains smaller than $0.1\,{\rm \mu m}$, leaving unclear the physical conditions required to form those grains with radii of order $1\,{\rm \mu m}$. We systematically investigate graphite nucleation and growth in expanding supernova ejecta by varying the explosion energy, ejecta mass, initial ejecta radius, and ejected $^{56}$Ni mass. We use a simplified one-zone model that follows the temperature and density evolution including adiabatic cooling, radiative cooling, and heating by radioactive nickel. We show that the final graphite grain size is mainly determined by the product of the mass density of atomic carbon available for grain growth and the local cooling timescale, both evaluated at a reference temperature of $2000\,{\rm K}$. Our models show that graphite growth is favored by lower explosion energy, larger ejecta mass, and smaller initial ejecta radius, which keep the gas denser near the graphite-condensation temperature. When radioactive heating and radiative cooling are included, explosions with $E_{\rm exp}\sim10^{50}\,{\rm erg}$ and $M_{\rm Ni}\lesssim10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ can form $1$-$10\,\mu{\rm m}$ graphite grains in the ejected helium layer or carbon-oxygen core, whereas $E_{\rm exp}\sim10^{51}\,{\rm erg}$ models do not. These results suggest that micron-sized presolar supernova graphite preferentially forms in faint-supernova-like explosions with low explosion energies, little ejected nickel, and helium layer or carbon-oxygen core ejecta.

2610.42132.abstract: We report on the results of our XMM-Newton and NuSTAR campaign targeting V1674 Her in October 2023. These observations were timed to investigate the post-nova quiescent state 28 months after the 2021 outburst, although the optical luminosity was still slowly declining. The X-ray spectra are well-modeled by a multi-temperature thermal plasma. While in the best fit temperature we find that the highest plasma temperature is indicative of a massive white dwarf ($M_{\text{WD}} \approx 1.35 M_\odot$), we caution that there is a degeneracy between the plasma temperature and the metallicity in the spectral fit, hindering a definitive constraint. Alternatively, the continuum can be phenomenologically described by a Comptonized component, although this model neglects the thermal bremsstrahlung component. Timing analysis reveals a stable 501.31 $\pm$ 0.19 s modulation in the post-quiescent phase, whose amplitude diminishes with increasing energy; this is quite typical in intermediate polars (IP). The phase alignment between the quiescent and early post-outburst Chandra spin-folded light curves suggests that the soft X-ray emission originates from the same polar regions, which quickly re-established accretion following the eruption. V1674 Her belongs to a growing class of novae that are also IPs, and is one of four in which the modulation with rotation was observed during the outburst supersoft X-ray phase. We propose that the fast rise in outburst was due to a fast or centrifugal magnetic rotator wind, causing rapid mass loss instead of the commonly assumed radiation pressure wind.

2610.40784.abstract: We present a galaxy-scale black hole (BH) accretion and feedback model incorporating results from multi-zone general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations spanning the event horizon to the Bondi radius. The model replaces a fixed suppression of the Bondi rate with a nuclear-environment-dependent factor, $\kappa^{\rm hot}_{\rm cho}$, set by the local ratio of Bondi to gravitational radius, and distributes outflow mass, kinetic energy, and thermal energy according to the angular structure measured in the large-dynamic-range GRMHD calculations. We apply it to idealized isolated simulations of an M87*-like massive elliptical and a Milky Way/Sgr A*-like galaxy, spanning over three orders of magnitude in BH mass without tuning accretion or feedback efficiencies to match observables. In the M87*-like system, the GRMHD-informed angle-dependent feedback model suppresses late-time stellar mass growth more effectively than the isotropic reference model, despite similar long-term BH accretion rates. Varying the uncertain mass loading of the collimated polar component has a modest impact on BH growth and star formation, indicating that feedback anisotropy matters more than its detailed mass loading. We find that $\kappa^{\rm hot}_{\rm cho}$ varies with nuclear environment and time, yielding BH growth histories markedly different from fixed-suppression models. For Sgr A*, this variable factor yields an accretion rate more consistent with Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) constraints than a fixed, suppressed Bondi model. These results show that nuclear-environment-dependent accretion and feedback angular structure affect BH-galaxy evolution, requiring subgrid models to include more than a universal Bondi suppression factor and a scalar feedback efficiency.

2610.40795.abstract: Black holes offer a unique setting to test gravity in the strong-field regime, where deviations from General Relativity are expected to be most pronounced. We study how modified gravity changes the structure of an advection-dominated accretion flow (ADAF) around a supermassive black hole. The gravitational field governing the disc is described by a Paczyński--Wiita-like potential derived in Eddington-inspired Born--Infeld (EiBI) gravity, formulated \textit{à la} Palatini. We solve the ADAF-like equations for this potential and compare the radial profiles of the flow with those obtained for the standard Paczyński--Wiita potential. The largest difference appears in the gas density, which is several orders of magnitude higher in the EiBI case near the inner region and converges to the standard result at large radii. The specific angular momentum and temperature are lower in EiBI gravity, while the radial velocity differs mainly at large radii for both solution branches, $ s=-1$ and $+1$. The angular velocity and the disk aspect ratio $H/r$ change only slightly. These results show that EiBI gravity can modify the density structure of hot accretion flows in the strong-field regime, potentially providing observational discriminators.

2610.40892.abstract: Self-diffusion in crystallized Coulomb (Yukawa) plasmas proceeds by the thermally activated formation of vacancy-interstitial pairs and the migration of these defects through the lattice, commonly known as Frenkel pairs in the materials literature. Molecular dynamics has recently resolved an Eyring law for diffusion in unstrained crystals, which we generalize to deformed crystals in this work. We simulate sheared Yukawa crystals and show that a static elastic strain exponentially enhances diffusion due to the additional elastic energy stored in the region that participates in Frenkel pair formation relative to the unstrained crystal: $D(\varepsilon)=D_0(\Gamma^{*})\exp[V^{*}\sigma/k_{\rm B}T]$, with $\sigma=\tfrac12\mu\varepsilon^{2}$ the elastic energy density stored by the shear strain $\varepsilon$ and $V^{*}$ the activation volume. We find a single activation volume $N_{\rm act} = n_iV^{*}\simeq31$ suffices for typical astrophysical screenings with a reduction at higher screening. This suggests Frenkel pair formation requires only a brief coordination of the nearest neighbors at a thermal maximum in oscillation. Stress-enhanced diffusion supplies a microphysical mechanism for creep in strained neutron star crusts and crystallizing white dwarf cores.

2610.41082.abstract: We investigate the equilibrium structure and stability against radial oscillations of a variety of two-fluid compact objects containing ordinary baryonic matter admixed with cold dark matter coupled through the background spacetime. For the ordinary fluid, we employ a QCD equation of state compatible with chiral effective field theory at nuclear densities (supplemented by the BPS and Negele-Vautherin models at extremely low densities) and with perturbative QCD in the high-density regime while also satisfying also current astrophysical data. For the dark fluid, we assume self-interacting fermionic matter with particle masses of $m_f=$ 2, 5, 10, and 100 GeV and two self-interaction strengths of $y=0.1$ and $10^3$. By scanning a large range of central pressures for both fluids, we identify the presence of dark compact planets, dark white dwarfs, dark neutron stars and the so-called dark oysters. Importantly, these objects are not only in two-fluid hydrostatic equilibrium, but they are also stable against two-fluid radial oscillations. We find that the relative representation of each class in the radially stable sample is strongly sensitive to the combinations of $m_f$ and $y$, with some combinations entirely suppressing some of these object classes within the sampled domain while favoring others. In addition to these classes, strong self-repulsion supports stable, dark-matter-dominated branches with compact ordinary-matter cores and extended dark halos, approaching the self-interacting fermion-star limit. Finally, we calculate the gravitational redshift at the ordinary-matter surface, $z_{\rm OM}$, including the contribution of extended dark-matter halos for which we found radially stable configurations with $z_{\rm OM}>2$.

2610.41229.abstract: Gravitational waves from eccentric compact binary coalescences trace dynamical binary formation, but matched-filtering searches responsible for most detections rely on quasicircular templates. Quantifying any sensitivity loss is crucial for assessing population completeness and the need for dedicated eccentric template banks. We present the first systematic GstLAL search study spanning eccentricities up to $e_{\rm 15Hz}=0.99$ and broad ranges of chirp mass, mass ratio, inclination, and aligned spin. Using TEOBResumS-Dalí waveforms, we inject eccentric signals and measure recovered signal-to-noise ratio, signal-consistency statistics, false-alarm rate, and sensitive volume and distance. For high-mass binaries ($\mathcal{M}_c\gtrsim30\,M_\odot$), sensitive distance is nearly independent of eccentricity, demonstrating that greater eccentricity does not necessarily reduce search sensitivity. In contrast, for low-mass binaries, sensitive distance falls by up to $\sim50\%$ near $e_{\rm 15Hz}\approx0.75$. Although the absolute loss in reach is modest given their low quasicircular sensitivity, this relative reduction exceeds the increase in sensitive distance between the second and third observing runs of the LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA collaboration and is consistent with previous low-mass studies. We also find that waveform matches at fixed source parameters substantially overpredict search sensitivity loss, meaning that the pipeline's signal-consistency test and maximization over its template bank mitigate much of the predicted sensitivity loss. This highlights the need for end-to-end injection campaigns to establish the detectability of eccentric binaries.

2610.41493.abstract: The magnetic Prandtl number ($\mathrm{Pm}$), the ratio of viscosity to magnetic diffusivity, spans many orders of magnitude in astrophysical plasmas. It shapes how turbulence amplifies and structures magnetic fields. In direct numerical simulations (DNS) the viscosity and magnetic diffusivity can be controlled explicitly and independently, whereas in implicit large eddy simulations (ILES) they are set by the numerical scheme. We test whether, in a finite-volume code, $\mathrm{Pm}$ can be varied through the reconstruction scheme by applying different methods to the hydro and magnetic variables. As a proof of concept, we simulate driven, subsonic, homogeneous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence using five pairs of hydrodynamic and magnetic reconstruction schemes at varying resolutions. We measure the effective viscosity and resistivity from the energy transfer between scales. Reconstructing the magnetic field at higher order than the fluid raises the effective magnetic Prandtl number and vice versa. We demonstrate that a mix of second- and third-order reconstruction alone results in a $\gtrsim20\times$ change in $\mathrm{Pm}$. A comparison of DNS with matched explicit dissipation at these values agrees with the ILES. Mixed reconstruction thus offers a simple and efficient way to explore $\mathrm{Pm} ot\simeq 1$ in ILES without adding explicit dissipation.

2610.41775.abstract: Dark100 is the first phase of an extensive array of Panoramic SETI (PANOSETI) telescopes at Palomar Observatory, California. PANOSETI telescopes are small, 0.5-m Fresnel lens telescopes instrumented with 1024-pixel silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) cameras. The telescopes were originally designed to search for ultra-fast optical transients, but they also function as cost-effective imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs). Dark100 will use seven of these widely separated IACTs to map the ultra-high-energy (UHE) gamma-ray sources on the Galactic Plane at high resolution. Dark100 will also leverage the IACT technique to search for evidence of ultra-heavy dark matter in a mass range that extends beyond 100 TeV. Deployment of the first four telescopes and enclosures was completed in December 2025, and commissioning of the next three is scheduled to finish by the end of 2026. The array has so far collected more than 100 hours of 3-telescope data on sources including the Crab Nebula and Markarian 421. Here we present the current status of Dark100.
